**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 5, 2026
**Re:** Breidoun Aviation Holdings, Inc. / Miriv Provisioning Group, LLC: Post-Closing Review of Deal Documents (Ostrander Skyline Catering, Inc.)

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed the four documents in the matter folder:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement dated June 15, 2026 (the "**SPA**");
- the Confirmatory IP Assignment Agreement dated September 25, 2026 (the "**IP Assignment**");
- the Key Employee Agreement with Renata Solvig dated July 1, 2026 (the "**KEA**"); and
- the Linen and Galley-Cart Washing Services Agreement with Pellacourt Linen Services LLC dated January 6, 2025 (the "**Pellacourt Agreement**").

I found four substantive issues. They are ranked below by risk to Breidoun, taking into account both the dollars at stake and how urgently we need to act.

| # | Issue | Location | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The Notice of Disagreement was delivered 16 days after the 30-day window. The Closing Statement risks becoming final and binding. | SPA §2.4(b); IP Assignment Recitals C–D | **Highest. Time-critical** |
| 2 | The IP Assignment pulls SPA §4.12 IP-rep breaches back under the 10% Cap. | IP Assignment §8.3; SPA §§9.5(a)–(b), 11.10 | **High** |
| 3 | The IP Assignment selects Delaware law and an exclusive Delaware Chancery forum, which conflicts with the SPA's New York law and New York County forum. The SPA precedence clause does not cure this. | IP Assignment §10; SPA §§11.8, 11.10 | **High** |
| 4 | The KEA's narrower "Business" definition leaves galley provisioning and crew meals outside Solvig's non-compete. | KEA §1, §7.1, §7.2; SPA §§1.1, 6.9 | **Medium-High** |

**Pellacourt Agreement.** Nothing in it bears on the issues above or requires action. See Part III.

Issues 2 and 3 both sit in the IP Assignment, and both take effect through SPA §11.10. Under that section, an Ancillary Agreement "controls as to its subject matter" in any conflict with the SPA. The IP Assignment is an Ancillary Agreement: it is an "IP Assignment Agreement" delivered under SPA §6.10, and its own Recital B says so. As a result, the SPA terms that protect Breidoun do not override these provisions. Breidoun signed the IP Assignment through its joinder (§9.1 expressly agrees to §§9–11). Any fix therefore requires a written amendment signed by Miriv, Ostrander and Breidoun (IP Assignment §11.3).

Because the IP Assignment is signed after the Notice of Disagreement dispute arose and records that dispute, it is likely the most efficient vehicle for addressing Issues 1–3 together. I recommend we propose a single amendment package.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Notice of Disagreement Delivered Outside the 30-Day Window (Highest Risk; Time-Critical)

**Where:** SPA §2.4(b), with §2.4(a), (c) and (e); IP Assignment Recitals C and D.

**What the documents say.**

- **Timeline.** Closing occurred July 1, 2026 (SPA §3.1). Seller delivered the Closing Statement on August 3, 2026 (IP Assignment Recital C). That was within the 45-day period in SPA §2.4(a).
- **The window.** Under SPA §2.4(b), Buyer may deliver a Notice of Disagreement "within 30 days after delivery of the Closing Statement." The period is stated in calendar days, not Business Days. Counting from August 3, it **expired on or about September 2, 2026**, a Wednesday and a Business Day.
- **Late delivery.** Breidoun delivered its Notice of Disagreement on September 18, 2026 (Recital D), roughly **16 days late**.
- **Consequence.** Section 2.4(b) states that if Buyer does not deliver a Notice of Disagreement within that period, "the Closing Statement and Seller's calculation of Closing Working Capital shall be final and binding on the Parties."
- **Current positions.** Recital D records that Seller "rejects the Notice of Disagreement as untimely" and that Buyer "expressly reserves its position."

**Why it matters to Breidoun.**

- **Price adjustment.** If the deemed-acceptance language applies, Seller's Closing Working Capital figure fixes the post-closing price adjustment under §2.4(e). Breidoun also loses access to the Independent Accountant process, because §2.4(c) is triggered only by a *timely* notice.
- **Payment obligation.** If Seller's figure exceeds the estimate used at Closing, Breidoun owes the excess within five Business Days after Closing Working Capital becomes final. Seller may argue that this date has already passed, and could assert a payment default.
- **Cap.** The final figure also sets the "Purchase Price" (SPA §2.2), which is the base for the 10% Cap. A lower Purchase Price lowers the Cap.
- **No easy fallback.** SPA §9.6 treats "determinations under Section 2.4" separately from indemnity. Breidoun may try to reframe the working capital items as breaches of the financial statement or undisclosed liabilities representations (§§4.5, 4.6). Seller will resist that route as an end-run around a final §2.4 determination. Any recovery that way would also be subject to the 0.75% basket (§9.5(c)) and the Cap.
- **What helps.** The reservation in Recital D helps. Breidoun has not accepted the Closing Statement, and SPA §11.5 requires any waiver to be in writing. But the reservation does not extend the deadline.

**Recommended fix.**

1. **Seek a written extension or tolling agreement from Seller now.** It should deem the September 18 notice timely. The simplest route is to fold it into the IP Assignment amendment we need anyway (Issues 2–3). Proposed language:

   > "Notwithstanding Section 2.4(b) of the Purchase Agreement, Seller and Buyer agree that the Notice of Disagreement delivered by Buyer on September 18, 2026 shall be deemed to have been timely delivered under Section 2.4(b), and the procedures in Section 2.4(c) shall apply to the disputed items set forth in that Notice of Disagreement, with the 20-day negotiation period commencing on the date of this Amendment. Seller waives any claim that the Closing Statement or Seller's calculation of Closing Working Capital has become final and binding by reason of the timing of that Notice of Disagreement."

2. **Test whether the 30-day period ever started to run.** In particular:
   - Was the Closing Statement delivered to the notice address and by a method permitted under SPA §11.1? Email delivery, for example, counts only "with confirmation of transmission."
   - Did it include the "reasonable supporting detail" that §2.4(a) requires?
   - Was it prepared under the Accounting Principles on Schedule 1.1(a)?

   A defective delivery may support an argument that the window opened later than August 3.

3. **Look for estoppel or course-of-dealing facts.** Examples would be Seller requests for more time, ongoing information exchanges, or statements that the deadline would not be enforced.

4. **Preserve the position.** Send a short reservation-of-rights letter, if one has not already gone out. It should confirm that Breidoun does not accept the Closing Statement and that no payment is due under §2.4(e) while the dispute is pending. Breidoun should not make any §2.4(e) payment without our review.

5. **Evaluate the indemnity fallback in parallel.** Assess whether the disputed items also support claims under §§4.5 or 4.6 within the 18-month survival period (§9.1).

**Open questions for the client:**

- How and to whom was the Closing Statement delivered on August 3, and what did it include?
- Why was the notice delivered on September 18? Did Seller do anything to cause or induce the delay?
- What is the dollar amount in dispute, and in which direction does it run (would Breidoun owe Seller, or Seller owe Breidoun)?
- Has Seller demanded payment under §2.4(e)?

---

### Issue 2: IP Assignment §8.3 Strips the IP Carve-Out from the Indemnity Cap (High Risk)

**Where:** IP Assignment §8.3; SPA §§9.5(a), 9.5(b), 11.10.

**What the documents say.**

- **The SPA bargain.** Under SPA §9.5(a), Seller's liability for representation breaches is capped at **10% of the Purchase Price** (the "Cap"). Section 9.5(b) carves out three categories from the Cap: Fraud, Fundamental Representations, and "any breach of the representations and warranties in Section 4.12 (Intellectual Property)." Those carved-out categories are instead capped at the full Purchase Price. Section 4.12 IP representations also survive until 60 days after the statute of limitations runs (§9.1).
- **What §8.3 does.** IP Assignment §8.3 provides that Assignor's aggregate liability "for Losses arising out of any breach of this Agreement or of the representations and warranties in Section 4.12 of the Purchase Agreement, whether claimed under this Agreement or under Article IX of the Purchase Agreement, shall be subject to the Cap set forth in Section 9.5(a) of the Purchase Agreement, **notwithstanding Section 9.5(b)** of the Purchase Agreement." It also provides that amounts paid under the IP Assignment count toward the Cap.
- **Why the SPA does not override it.** Section 8.3 deals expressly with liability for IP matters. That is squarely the IP Assignment's subject matter, so it controls under SPA §11.10.

**Why it matters to Breidoun.**

- **The core assets.** The Recipes and Specifications and the Ostrander Marks are the core value of a catering business. The SPA deliberately exposed Seller to Purchase-Price-level liability for defects in title to them.
- **Effect of §8.3.** Section 8.3 converts that exposure into a 10% ceiling, which is shared with every other general rep claim. If a third party (or a Seller Affiliate) asserts ownership of the recipes or the brand, Breidoun's recovery is now limited to 10% of the Purchase Price instead of up to 100%.
- **Uncapped items that remain.** Because §8.3 counts IP Assignment payments toward the Cap, a claim under the new §8.1 indemnity also uses up capacity that would otherwise be available for unrelated rep breaches. The only carve-outs left are Fraud (§8.3, last sentence) and, arguably, breaches of Seller covenants such as §6.10.
- **No consideration received.** Breidoun appears to have given this up for nothing. IP Assignment §2.4 confirms that no new consideration passed, and SPA §6.10 obliged Seller to deliver the confirmatory assignment "without further consideration" and "[w]ithout limiting Section 4.12."

**Recommended fix.** Amend the IP Assignment to delete §8.3 and replace it with the following:

> "**8.3 Relationship to Purchase Agreement Limitations.** Nothing in this Agreement limits, reduces or otherwise modifies Section 9.5(b) of the Purchase Agreement. Losses arising out of any breach of this Agreement or of the representations and warranties in Section 4.12 of the Purchase Agreement are not subject to the Cap and are subject only to the limitation in the last sentence of Section 9.5(b) of the Purchase Agreement. Amounts paid under this Agreement do not count toward the Cap. In the event of any conflict between this Section 8.3 and any other provision of this Agreement or the Purchase Agreement, including Section 11.10 of the Purchase Agreement, this Section 8.3 controls."

As fallback arguments if Seller refuses:

- Seller's insistence on §8.3 contradicts its covenant to deliver the assignment "without further consideration" and "without limiting Section 4.12." This supports a covenant claim under SPA §9.2(b), which is not subject to the Cap because §9.5(a) caps only §9.2(a).
- We may also have an argument that SPA §11.10 resolves "conflicts" only as to the Ancillary Agreement's subject matter (title to IP), not the SPA's indemnity architecture. I consider this argument weak given §8.3's express "notwithstanding" language, and I would not rely on it.

**Open questions for the client:**

- Who negotiated the IP Assignment for Breidoun, and was §8.3 a conscious trade (for example, for the Recipes and Specifications delivery in §3, or for something else)?
- Is Breidoun aware of any actual or threatened IP title issue? The Buyer request that triggered §6.10 suggests Breidoun believed Seller or an Affiliate "holds or may hold" an interest. That is the exact risk §8.3 now caps.

---

### Issue 3: Delaware Law and Exclusive Delaware Forum in the IP Assignment Conflict with the SPA (High Risk)

**Where:** IP Assignment §10.1 and §10.2; SPA §§11.8, 11.10.

**What the documents say.**

- **The SPA.** SPA §11.8 provides that the SPA is governed by **New York law**. It also provides that each Party submits to "the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in New York County, New York, for disputes under any Transaction Document." The IP Assignment is itself a Transaction Document.
- **The IP Assignment.** IP Assignment §10.1 selects "the laws of the State of Delaware" for the agreement "and all claims and causes of action arising out of or relating to it or to the Assigned IP." Section 10.2 provides for "the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware" for any proceeding "arising out of or relating to this Agreement or the Assigned IP," with Delaware Superior Court or the District of Delaware as fallbacks. Breidoun agreed to §10 in its joinder (§9.1).
- **Why the SPA does not cure the conflict.** Under SPA §11.10, the Ancillary Agreement "controls as to its subject matter." Governing law and forum for disputes about the Assigned IP fall within that subject matter. **The SPA's New York clause therefore does not override the Delaware clause as to IP matters.** The general rule that the SPA controls applies only "otherwise."

**Why it matters to Breidoun.**

- **One set of facts, two forums.** A single factual event, such as a claim that the recipes or the Ostrander Marks were never owned by Ostrander, may give rise to two different proceedings:
  - a claim under IP Assignment §§7–8, or any dispute "relating to … the Assigned IP," which goes to Delaware Chancery under Delaware law; and
  - an SPA Article IX indemnity claim for breach of §4.12, which goes to New York County under New York law.
- **Risk of parallel proceedings.** Seller can use the "relating to … the Assigned IP" language to move to dismiss or stay a New York indemnity action, or to start a pre-emptive Delaware declaratory action. Breidoun then faces:
  - parallel proceedings and duplicated cost;
  - the risk of inconsistent findings on title, damages and the effect of §8.3;
  - procedural fights over which clause governs; and
  - possible differences in contract-construction rules (including how each state treats limitation-of-liability and "notwithstanding" language).
- **Exposure to Breidoun's own claims.** Breidoun, as joinder party, is itself bound to sue in Delaware on IP claims, even though it is a New York corporation and the target, its commissaries and the other deal documents are all New York-based.

**Recommended fix.** In the same amendment, replace §10.1 and §10.2 with language that conforms to SPA §11.8:

> "**10.1 Governing Law.** This Agreement, and all claims and causes of action arising out of or relating to it or to the Assigned IP, shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of New York, without regard to conflict of laws principles that would require application of the laws of another jurisdiction.
>
> **10.2 Exclusive Forum.** Each of Assignor, Assignee and Buyer irrevocably submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in New York County, New York, for any action or proceeding arising out of or relating to this Agreement, the Assigned IP or the Purchase Agreement, and waives any objection to venue in those courts and any claim that those courts are an inconvenient forum. Nothing in this Section 10.2 limits any Party's right to record this Agreement or to bring any registration, opposition or cancellation proceeding before the United States Patent and Trademark Office or any other registry."

**Alternative.** If Seller will not reopen §10, amend SPA §11.10 (by an SPA amendment under §11.4, signed by both Parties) to carve governing law and forum out of the precedence rule:

> "…the Ancillary Agreement controls as to its subject matter; *provided* that Section 11.8 and Section 11.9 of this Agreement shall control over any governing law, jurisdiction, forum or jury-waiver provision of any Ancillary Agreement; otherwise this Agreement controls."

**Interim step.** Pending amendment, any IP-related claim should be planned with both clauses in mind. Where possible, Breidoun should frame claims under SPA §9.2 (for breach of §4.12) and avoid invoking IP Assignment §§7–8.

**Open question:** Did Seller propose the Delaware clause, and did Breidoun's team flag the conflict with SPA §11.8 at signing? The answer bears on negotiating leverage.

---

### Issue 4: Narrower "Business" Definition in Solvig's Key Employee Agreement (Medium-High Risk)

**Where:** KEA §1 ("Business"), §7.1 (Non-Competition), §7.2 (Non-Solicitation of Customers); SPA §§1.1, 6.9, 11.10.

**What the documents say.**

- **The SPA definition.** SPA §1.1 defines "Business" as "**inflight catering, galley provisioning and crew meal services for regional air carriers**." That matches Ostrander's three service lines (SPA Recital B).
- **The SPA covenant.** SPA §6.9 requires Seller to cause the Key Employee to sign a KEA with a covenant "not to engage in the Business" for at least two years after termination.
- **The KEA definition.** KEA §1 defines "Business" as only "**the preparation of hot inflight meals for regional air carriers**."
- **Effect on the restrictive covenants.** KEA §7.1 restricts Solvig only from working for a Person "engaged in the Business." KEA §7.2(a) restricts her only from soliciting Customers for "products or services of the Business."
- **Precedence.** The KEA is an Ancillary Agreement, so under SPA §11.10 its own definition controls as to its subject matter.

**Why it matters to Breidoun.** Solvig is Executive Chef and General Manager. She manages carrier relationships (KEA §2.2) and has full access to the Recipes and Specifications, galley loading plans and pricing. Under the KEA as written, after she leaves she may:

- join or found a competitor in **galley provisioning** and **crew meal services**, two of the three acquired service lines, anywhere in the United States; and
- solicit Ostrander's carrier customers for those services, and arguably for cold or non-hot inflight items as well.

The confidentiality covenant (KEA §6) and the employee non-solicit (KEA §7.3) still apply. But confidentiality covenants are harder to police than a non-compete. The goodwill Breidoun paid for is therefore materially under-protected.

**Recommended fix.**

1. **Amend the KEA** (KEA §11.6 requires signature by Solvig and an authorized Company officer). Replace the definition in §1 with:

   > "'**Business**' means inflight catering, galley provisioning and crew meal services for regional air carriers, including the preparation, assembly and supply of hot and cold inflight meals, snacks and beverages, galley provisioning and loading, and crew meal services, and any other business conducted by the Company as of the Effective Date or the Termination Date."

   Because Solvig must agree, we should offer fresh consideration to support enforceability. Options include a supplemental retention or bonus amount, or an increase to the second retention installment under §4.3. Continued employment alone may be challenged. Before finalizing, we should also confirm the current status of New York law and any federal developments on non-competes, since I have not verified whether any recent change affects enforceability.

2. **Preserve a claim against Seller under SPA §6.9.** The KEA delivered at Closing does not include a covenant not to engage in the "Business" as the SPA defines it. That is a breach of a Seller covenant, which is indemnifiable under SPA §9.2(b). That claim is **not subject to the Cap or the basket**, which apply only to §9.2(a). Breidoun should send a written claim notice under SPA §9.4. It should also ask Seller to cooperate in obtaining the amendment, including by funding any additional consideration Solvig requires.

3. **Interim protection.** Until the amendment is signed, the Company should strictly enforce KEA §§5.6, 6.1 and 7.3 and document Solvig's access to Confidential Information. That record supports trade-secret protection independent of the non-compete.

**Open questions for the client:**

- What is Solvig's current status and retention outlook? Is there any indication she may leave?
- Did Breidoun's team review the KEA definition before Closing? Seller may argue that Breidoun waived the §6.9 breach by closing on a KEA it received under §3.2(a)(ii) and the §7.1(d) condition.
- Did Solvig receive transaction proceeds? KEA §7.5 refers to "her proceeds from … the transactions." If she did, the non-compete may be analyzed under the more lenient sale-of-business standard.

---

## III. Pellacourt Linen and Galley-Cart Washing Services Agreement

**Conclusion: nothing in the Pellacourt Agreement affects the issues above, and it does not require action in connection with this post-closing review.**

- **No transfer problem.** This was a stock purchase, so Ostrander remains the contracting party. The agreement has no change-of-control or anti-assignment trigger implicated by the deal (§11.2 restricts only assignment and permits the Customer to assign to affiliates and successors).
- **Consistent law and forum.** It is governed by **New York law** with a New York County forum (§11.5), consistent with the SPA.
- **No bearing on the identified issues.** It does not touch IP ownership, the Closing Statement or the Key Employee.
- **Ordinary commercial terms.** Its terms are customer-favorable: CPI-capped price increases of no more than 4% (§4.2), vendor risk of loss (§5), insurance with Ostrander as additional insured (§7), vendor indemnity (§8.1), and confidentiality covering customer identities, flight schedules and pricing (§9). Ostrander can terminate for convenience on 120 days' notice (§6.4).

**Minor housekeeping points (low risk; for the client's operations team, not the deal fix):**

- Confirm that the agreement was listed on Disclosure Schedule §4.8 as a Material Contract (it is a "supplier of … linen … or galley services" contract). If it was omitted, that is a minor §4.8 point only.
- Calendar the initial term end date (January 6, 2028) and the 90-day non-renewal deadline (§6.1).
- Confirm that current insurance certificates are on file (§7.2).

---

## IV. Consolidated Open Questions for the Client

1. Closing Statement: method of delivery, recipient, and contents on August 3, 2026.
2. Reason for the September 18 timing of the Notice of Disagreement, and any Seller communications on the deadline.
3. Amount and direction of the working capital dispute; whether Seller has demanded a §2.4(e) payment.
4. Background to IP Assignment §§8.3 and 10: who negotiated them, and whether they were traded for anything.
5. Whether any actual or suspected IP title issue prompted the §6.10 request.
6. Solvig's status, retention outlook, and whether she received transaction proceeds.
7. Whether the KEA "Business" definition was reviewed before Closing.

## V. Recommended Next Steps

1. **Immediately:** send Seller a reservation-of-rights letter on the Closing Statement, if not already sent, and request a tolling agreement.
2. **Within one week:** propose a single Amendment No. 1 to the IP Assignment, signed by Miriv, Ostrander and Breidoun, that:
   - deems the Notice of Disagreement timely (Issue 1);
   - replaces §8.3 (Issue 2); and
   - conforms §10 to New York law and forum (Issue 3).
3. **In parallel:**
   - deliver a SPA §9.4 claim notice to Seller for the §6.9 breach;
   - approach Solvig, through the Company, with a KEA amendment and supporting consideration (Issue 4); and
   - confirm the current enforceability landscape for non-competes in New York.

Please let me know if you would like me to prepare drafts of the amendment, the reservation-of-rights letter or the §9.4 claim notice.

- **Loss of the adjustment.** If Seller's position holds, the Closing Statement is final and binding. Closing Working Capital would be fixed at Seller's figures, and Breidoun loses any downward adjustment it believes it is owed under §2.4(e).
- **No indemnity backstop.** SPA §9.6 carves "determinations under Section 2.4" out of the exclusive-remedy provision. Seller will argue that this confirms §2.4 is a self-contained mechanism. Breidoun should expect resistance to any attempt to re-run working-capital disputes as indemnity claims under §9.2.
- **Admission risk.** Breidoun signed the IP Assignment joinder, and the IP Assignment records the dates and Seller's objection. Breidoun has therefore acknowledged the underlying dates in a signed instrument. The reservation in Recital D preserves Breidoun's position but does not cure the lateness.

**Possible arguments to preserve the dispute.** Each of these depends on facts we need from the client (see Open Questions):

1. **Delivery defects.** Was the August 3 delivery a valid "delivery" under SPA §11.1? That section requires personal delivery, overnight courier (deemed given one Business Day after deposit) or email with confirmation of transmission, sent to the addresses on the signature page. The SPA signature-page notice blocks in our copy are blank. If Seller sent the Closing Statement to the wrong person or address, or without confirmation of transmission, the 30-day clock may have started later or not at all.
2. **Insufficient supporting detail.** SPA §2.4(a) requires the Closing Statement to include "reasonable supporting detail." If it did not, Breidoun can argue that a compliant Closing Statement was never delivered and the clock never ran.
3. **Waiver or estoppel.** Did Seller agree to an extension, engage on the merits after September 2, or otherwise induce the delay? Under SPA §11.5, a waiver must be in writing and signed, but correspondence may still support an estoppel argument.
4. **Accounting Principles.** If Seller's calculation departs from the Accounting Principles in Schedule 1.1(a), the "final and binding" language may not protect a calculation that was not prepared in accordance with the SPA. This is a weaker argument.

**Recommendation:**

- **Gather facts immediately.** Before any further correspondence with Seller, obtain the transmittal of the Closing Statement (date, method, recipient, attachments) and all correspondence from August 3 through September 18.
- **Seek a written extension or tolling agreement.** If we have any delivery or content argument, approach Seller promptly. Proposed language:

  > "Seller and Buyer agree that, notwithstanding Section 2.4(b) of the Stock Purchase Agreement, the Notice of Disagreement delivered by Buyer on September 18, 2026 shall be deemed timely delivered for all purposes of Section 2.4, and the disputed items specified in it shall be resolved in accordance with Section 2.4(c). Seller waives any objection to the timeliness of the Notice of Disagreement."

Nothing should be said or signed that accepts the Closing Statement or treats it as final.

### Issue 2: IP Assignment Pulls IP Representation Breaches Under the 10% Cap

**Where:** IP Assignment §8.3, read with SPA §§9.5(a), 9.5(b) and 11.10.

**What the documents say:**

- **The SPA bargain.** SPA §9.5(a) caps Seller's liability for representation breaches at 10% of the Purchase Price (the "Cap"). SPA §9.5(b)(iii) excludes breaches of §4.12 (Intellectual Property) from the Cap and subjects them only to an overall ceiling equal to the Purchase Price. The §4.12 representations also survive until 60 days after the statute of limitations (SPA §9.1).
- **The IP Assignment change.** IP Assignment §8.3 provides that Assignor's aggregate liability for Losses "arising out of any breach of this Agreement **or of the representations and warranties in Section 4.12 of the Purchase Agreement**, whether claimed under this Agreement or under Article IX of the Purchase Agreement, shall be **subject to the Cap set forth in Section 9.5(a)** of the Purchase Agreement, **notwithstanding Section 9.5(b)** of the Purchase Agreement." It also provides that amounts paid under the IP Assignment count toward the Cap. Only Fraud is preserved.
- **Why §8.3 likely prevails.** Under SPA §11.10, the IP Assignment controls as to its subject matter. The subject matter of §8.3 is liability for Company Intellectual Property title and the §4.12 representations. Seller will say that falls squarely within the IP Assignment's scope.

**Why it matters:**

- **The protected risk has been capped.** Ostrander's core value lies in its recipes, menu specifications, galley loading plans and the Ostrander Skyline marks. The §4.12 carve-out was the buyer's principal protection against defective title to exactly those assets. §8.3 reduces Breidoun's recovery for an IP title failure from up to the full Purchase Price to 10% of it.
- **Erosion of the general Cap.** Because IP losses now count toward the same Cap, an IP claim also uses up the Cap that is otherwise available for every general representation breach, including financial statements, material contracts and compliance.
- **No apparent consideration.** IP Assignment §2.4 confirms no additional consideration was paid. SPA §6.10 obligates Seller to deliver the confirmatory assignment "without further consideration" and "[w]ithout limiting Section 4.12." Seller has therefore used a document it was already obliged to deliver to take back a negotiated SPA protection.

**Counter-arguments available to Breidoun.** These are not strong enough to rely on:

- **Joinder scope.** Under IP Assignment §9.1, Buyer joined only "to accept the benefit of Sections 7 and 8, and to agree to Sections 9, 10 and 11." A limitation on Seller's liability is not a "benefit" to Buyer. Breidoun can therefore argue that it never agreed to §8.3 and that §8.3 does not satisfy the SPA §11.4 requirement that amendments be signed by each Party.
- **SPA §6.10.** The confirmatory assignment was to be "without limiting Section 4.12." Breidoun can argue that §8.3 is outside what §6.10 contemplated and is not a true "conflict" that §11.10 resolves in the IP Assignment's favour.

Seller will respond that Buyer signed the instrument, that §8.3 is express and specific, and that §11.10 gives it effect. We should not assume the carve-out survives.

**Recommendation:**

- **Preferred fix.** Delete §8.3 and replace it with:

  > "**8.3 No Limitation of Purchase Agreement Remedies.** Nothing in this Agreement limits, reduces or otherwise modifies any right or remedy of Buyer or any other Buyer Indemnitee under the Purchase Agreement, including Sections 9.1, 9.5(b) and 9.6 of the Purchase Agreement. Losses arising out of any breach of this Agreement or of Section 4.12 of the Purchase Agreement are not subject to the Cap or the basket in Section 9.5(c) of the Purchase Agreement, and are subject only to the limitation in the last sentence of Section 9.5(b) of the Purchase Agreement."

- **Fallback.** Add a carve-out to SPA §11.10, by amendment signed under SPA §11.4:

  > "...provided, however, that no Ancillary Agreement shall limit, cap or otherwise modify the indemnification obligations of Seller under Article IX of this Agreement unless such Ancillary Agreement expressly refers to this proviso."

- **Pressure points.** If Seller resists, Breidoun can rely on SPA §6.10 (delivery "without further consideration" and "without limiting Section 4.12") and SPA §6.8 (further assurances).

### Issue 3: Delaware Governing Law and Exclusive Delaware Forum in the IP Assignment

**Where:** IP Assignment §§10.1 and 10.2, against SPA §§11.8 and 11.10.

**What the documents say:**

- **The SPA.** SPA §11.8 selects New York law. It submits the parties to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in New York County "for disputes under any Transaction Document." The IP Assignment is a Transaction Document.
- **The IP Assignment.** IP Assignment §10.1 selects "the laws of the State of Delaware" for the agreement "and all claims and causes of action arising out of or relating to it **or to the Assigned IP**." Section 10.2 submits Assignor, Assignee and Buyer (Buyer is bound through the §9.1 joinder) to "the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware," with fallback to the Delaware Superior Court or the District of Delaware, for any action "arising out of or relating to this Agreement or the Assigned IP."
- **No cure from the SPA.** SPA §11.10 gives the Ancillary Agreement control "as to its subject matter." Governing law and forum for IP disputes are within the IP Assignment's subject matter. The SPA's New York clause therefore **does not override** the Delaware clause as to IP matters. On IP disputes, Delaware is likely to govern.

**Why it matters:**

- **Two forums for one set of facts.** Take a claim that Seller or an Affiliate retained rights in the recipes or marks. Title, specific performance (IP Assignment §8.4) and indemnity under IP Assignment §8.1 go to Delaware Chancery under Delaware law. An indemnity claim under SPA §9.2 for breach of §4.12 on the same facts goes to New York County under New York law. Breidoun faces **parallel proceedings**, duplicated cost, and the risk of inconsistent findings on the same facts.
- **Pull of the broad clause.** The phrase "or to the Assigned IP" in §10.2 is broad. Seller could argue that even SPA §4.12 indemnity claims "relate to" the Assigned IP and must be brought in Delaware. That would undercut the SPA's exclusive New York forum entirely, and Delaware law (not New York law) could then govern the interpretation of IP Assignment §8.3 (Issue 2).
- **Fraud definition mismatch.** "Fraud" is defined in SPA §1.1 by reference to New York law. IP Assignment §8.3 preserves Fraud, but disputes about it may be heard by a Delaware court applying Delaware law to an IP-related claim. This adds uncertainty.
- **Practical burden.** Breidoun, the Company and the business are all in New York, so a Delaware forum is a practical burden on the client.

**Recommendation:**

- **Preferred fix.** Amend IP Assignment §10 to conform to the SPA:

  > "**10.1 Governing Law.** This Agreement, and all claims and causes of action arising out of or relating to it or to the Assigned IP, shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of New York, without regard to conflict of laws principles that would require application of the laws of another jurisdiction.
  >
  > **10.2 Exclusive Forum.** Each of Assignor, Assignee and Buyer irrevocably submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in New York County, New York, for any action or proceeding arising out of or relating to this Agreement or the Assigned IP, in accordance with Section 11.8 of the Purchase Agreement, and waives any objection to venue in those courts and any claim that those courts are an inconvenient forum."

- **Fallback.** Amend SPA §11.10 so that governing law and forum are always taken from the SPA:

  > "...provided, however, that Section 11.8 of this Agreement shall control over any governing law, jurisdiction or forum provision of any Ancillary Agreement."

- **Packaging.** Address this together with Issue 2 in a single amendment to the IP Assignment, signed by Assignor, Assignee and Buyer under IP Assignment §11.3. Recordation filings under IP Assignment §5 can proceed in the meantime, because the conveyance itself in §2.2 is not affected.
